section: 1.  Identify the most-recent date tag among saved CSVs
grain_out: one file per base name (9 bases)
operation: Lists CSVs in results/ whose name matches one of nine base names plus a date suffix, parses base and date from the filename, and keeps the single newest file per base; this is a filter on which result version is analysed, and the missing_bases warning block is absorbed because it only reports bases with no file and changes nothing.
settings: base_names fixed to 9 strings; filename must match ^(base)_dddd-dd-dd.csv$ exactly (no other suffixes); arrange(base, desc(date), desc(fname)) then slice_head(n = 1), so ties on date are broken by the lexically largest filename; the second filter(base %in% base_names) is redundant with the regex.
na_behavior: A filename whose date fails as.Date becomes NA and sorts last, so a malformed date can never be chosen but is not reported; a base with no file is dropped with a warning only, and later code that expects the object (line 154 for gamma_div) will then error; only gamma_div is used downstream, so the other 8 selections have no effect on this script.
notes: This is mostly a standard code I developed for general coding.

section: 2. Read each latest file into a named list
inputs: e1_regional_gamma.latest_file_per_base; INPUT:L5_gamma_diversity_observed_<date>.csv (and 8 other <base>_<date>.csv files that are read but not used in this script)
grain_out: gamma_div: one row per period x season (possibly x major_area; see question)
units_out: diversity values as stored in the CSV: richness (species count) and shannon (index)
operation: Reads each selected CSV with readr::read_csv and binds the tables to global names; the deframe, list2env, the nine rename assignments (lines 153 to 161) and the rm() cleanup are absorbed because they only carry the tables forward under new names. Question: the block comment at line 182 says gamma_div is indexed by major_area, period, season and holds rarefied_richness and rarefied_shannon, but the code downstream uses columns richness and shannon and never references major_area; which columns the file actually holds, and whether one row is a single subregion or the whole region, cannot be told from this script.
settings: read_csv with default column type guessing (first 1000 rows) and default na = c("", "NA"); show_col_types = FALSE only silences messages.
na_behavior: Empty cells and the string NA both become NA and are indistinguishable afterwards; period is read as character unless the file stores it otherwise, which matters for the join at line 260; if a selected base is absent the corresponding rename at lines 153 to 161 errors out.
notes: If anything, there should be errors for these code.

section: 1. REGIONAL TREND IN gamma-DIVERSITY / Prepare data
grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)
grain_out: same rows, with numeric mid_year attached
units_out: same, plus mid_year in calendar years
operation: Left-joins a lookup mapping period labels P1 to P11 onto mid-years 1993, 1996, ..., 2023 and converts season to a factor; the join is the node because it defines the time axis for every model below, and the season factor is absorbed because it only fixes level order (which is overridden again at line 502).
settings: 11 periods assumed, mid_year = seq(1993, 2023, by = 3), so P1 is taken to be 1992 to 1994 per the comment; period lookup is a factor joined to whatever type gamma_div$period has; season levels Winter, Spring, Summer, Fall.
na_behavior: Any period label not in P1..P11 (or a 12th period) gets mid_year NA silently and is later dropped by the lm filter and by gam's na.omit, so a label mismatch and a genuinely missing value look the same downstream; any season string not in the four levels becomes NA silently; if gamma_div$period is not character or factor the join errors.
notes: I decided to use three years for statistical reasons.

section: 1. REGIONAL TREND IN gamma-DIVERSITY / Linear regression results (ALL SEASONS COMBINED ONLY)
grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)
units_out: slope in metric units per year; SE of slope; q-value (proportion); n rows used
operation: Defines a function that drops rows with non-finite response or mid_year, fits an ordinary linear regression of the metric on mid_year pooled across all seasons (and areas, if present), and returns slope, SE, n and a BH-adjusted p-value; the filter and the fit are kept in one region because the function is the unit, and the filter is the part that changes which population the slope describes.
settings: Formula response ~ mid_year with no season term; p.adjust(method = "BH") on a single p-value, which equals the raw p (code and comment agree); coefficient extracted by name mid_year; no weights.
na_behavior: Rows with NA, NaN or Inf in either variable are removed silently; n in the output is the only trace of how many were dropped, and it does not distinguish a missing metric from a missing mid_year (e.g. an unmapped period label); with fewer than 3 usable rows the SE lookup errors or returns NA.
notes: It can be compacted; otherwise, it is okay.

section: 1. REGIONAL TREND IN gamma-DIVERSITY / Linear regression results (ALL SEASONS COMBINED ONLY)
grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)
units_out: species per year; SE; q-value; n
operation: Applies the pooled linear trend to richness; the section header promises per-season regressions but the code only fits the all-seasons-combined model.
settings: response = richness; everything else inherited from lm_overall_fn.

section: 1. REGIONAL TREND IN gamma-DIVERSITY / Linear regression results (ALL SEASONS COMBINED ONLY)
grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)
grain_out: lm_results: one row per metric (2 rows)
units_out: index units per year; SE; q-value; n
operation: Applies the pooled linear trend to shannon; the bind_rows into lm_results and the print are absorbed because they only stack the two one-row tables. Note the two q-values are adjusted separately (each over one test), not jointly across the two metrics.
settings: response = shannon; everything else inherited from lm_overall_fn.
na_behavior: As lm_overall_fn; the richness and shannon rows may rest on different n if missingness differs, and lm_results shows that only through the n column.

start_anchor: gam_richness <- mgcv::gam(richness ~ s(mid_year, by = season) + season,
end_context: gam_richness <- mgcv::gam(richness ~ s(mid_year, by = season) + season,
grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)
grain_out: one fitted model object (4 season-specific smooths plus season intercepts)
units_in: richness as species count; mid_year in years
units_out: model coefficients and smooth functions in richness units
operation: Fits a Gaussian GAM of richness on a separate smooth of mid_year for each season plus a season main effect, pooling across areas if more than one is present. Question: with at most 11 distinct mid_year values per season the default basis dimension k = 10 leaves almost no freedom for penalisation; is that intended?
settings: family gaussian with identity link on a count response; s(mid_year, by = season) with default bs = "tp", k = 10; method = "REML"; season as a factor with the level order set at line 262 (Winter first, so Winter is the reference intercept); na.action = na.omit by default.
na_behavior: Rows with NA in richness, mid_year or season are dropped silently before fitting; the model object records the number used (nobs) but not why rows were lost; a season with too few points makes the fit fail or the smooth collapse to linear without a warning specific to that season.
notes: Smooth and intercapts should be different among seasons as written. REML is fine.

grain_out: one row per season x grid point (4 x 100 = 400 rows)
units_out: predicted richness (species) and its standard error on the response scale
operation: Builds a prediction grid of 100 evenly spaced mid_year values per season spanning that season's observed range (an aggregation: min and max per season), then predicts richness with standard errors from gam_richness; the mutate that attaches fit and se.fit is absorbed because it only carries the predict() output onto the grid.
settings: length.out = 100 per season; range is min to max of observed mid_year within each season, so seasons with different coverage get different x ranges; predict with se.fit = TRUE, type = link (identity, so equal to response); no extrapolation.
na_behavior: If any mid_year is NA within a season, min and max return NA and seq() errors; if a season level exists in the factor but has no rows it gets no grid rows; predict returns NA for a season level absent from the fitted model.
notes: This is just to create smooth predicted values for plotting. This should be fine.

grain_in: one row per period x season (x major_area?)

units_out: model coefficients and smooth functions in index units
operation: Fits the same GAM structure as gam_richness with shannon as the response; same pooling and basis-dimension question applies.

grain_out: one row per season x grid point (400 rows)
units_out: predicted shannon (index) and its standard error
operation: Predicts shannon with standard errors on the grid built in pred_richness; reuses that grid, so the x range per season comes from the richness node even if shannon has different missingness; the mutate is absorbed for the same reason as in pred_richness.
settings: As pred_richness; pred_grid is not rebuilt.

inputs: called with e1_regional_gamma.gam_richness / e1_regional_gamma.gam_shannon (see call-site nodes)
grain_out: one row per model term (parametric and smooth)
units_out: estimate and SE in metric units (parametric rows only); edf; t or F statistic; p and BH q-value (proportions)
operation: Defines a function that calls summary() on a gam, reshapes the parametric and smooth coefficient tables into one long tibble, and adds a BH-adjusted q-value across all rows of that one model; the two transmute blocks and the empty-tibble fallbacks are absorbed because they only reformat summary() output. The definition is repeated verbatim starting at the second occurrence of the line extract_gam_summary <- function(model, metric) { (line 385); that second copy overwrites the first with identical code, so it is the same node, and the second region (lines 385 to 437) is intentionally left outside every region.
settings: p.adjust(method = "BH") over the parametric rows (intercept and 3 season contrasts) plus the 4 smooth rows of a single model, so the family of tests is per metric and includes the intercept; arrange(metric, component, term); statistic column mixes t (parametric) and F (smooth).
na_behavior: edf is NA for parametric rows and estimate/std.error are NA for smooth rows by construction; a NULL or empty p.table or s.table yields zero rows rather than an error, so a model with no smooth terms is not flagged; p.adjust drops NA p-values from the count of tests silently.

grain_out: one row per term of the richness model (8 rows)
operation: Applies the summary extractor to gam_richness; the identical call is made again at rich_summ <- extract_gam_summary(gam_richness, "Richness") (line 441) and produces the same table, so it is the same node.

grain_out: gam_summary_table: one row per term per metric (16 rows)
operation: Applies the summary extractor to gam_shannon and stacks it under the richness table; the bind_rows is absorbed because it only stacks. The call is repeated at shan_summ <- extract_gam_summary(gam_shannon, "Shannon") (line 442, differing only in a space) and the stacking at line 445; the later gam_summary_compact (lines 449 to 450) selects all nine columns in the same order and is a no-op, so it is left outside every region. Note q-values are adjusted within each metric, not across the 16 rows.
